claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 in the reported as-cast state has a hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations and hierarchical phase separation.
The reported hierarchical-heterostructured state can be obtained by standard arc melting and casting.
A machine-learning model can fuse XRD, SEM/BSE, nanoindentation, and small-scale tensile descriptors to predict bulk Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness.
Phase heterogeneities and multilevel chemical fluctuations govern dislocation mobility and crack initiation in HfNbTiVAl10.
Nanoindentation and microstructural-imaging descriptors capture the influence of chemical fluctuations on slip behavior and crack resistance.
Empirical scale-bridging descriptors can reproduce the physical trends governing elasticity, plastic yield, and fracture behavior.
Using empirical descriptors in the machine-learning framework reduces the need for computationally intensive first-principles calculations.
The integrated model will predict Young's modulus within ±10% error.
The integrated model will predict yield strength within ±15% error.
The integrated model will predict fracture toughness within ±15–20% error.
The integrated model will reduce computational time by at least one order of magnitude relative to high-fidelity CALPHAD and first-principles calculations.
The integrated model will have lower prediction errors than conventional first-principles and CALPHAD approaches.
Conventional thermophysical, CALPHAD, first-principles, and previous machine-learning methods have high computational costs and limited capability for predicting fracture properties.
The model's reliability may diminish when processing, grain-size distributions, or post-casting treatments alter the microstructural features used as inputs.
Scale effects and processing-history changes may limit the model's applicability.
The proposed ±10–20% error bounds are based on analogous high-entropy-alloy studies.

contradictions.description: The predicted yield-strength target is stated as ±15%, whereas the rejection rule groups yield strength with a looser ±15–20% range.
